title: Consumption Transition: Quick Reference Decision Matrix and Migration Checklist
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary

This page is a compact, operational reference for product managers, solutions engineers, and customer success teams leading a customer from Hosted to Dedicated or Edge consumption. It bundles: a decision matrix for choosing migration modes, a pre-migration checklist, cost and latency simulation knobs, a phased rollout plan, and a minimal set of contractual/SLA negotiation talking points. The goal is to reduce cycle time for migration while protecting customer SLAs and Redwood unit economics.

Who this is for
- Solutions engineering (primary)
- Customer success and account executives
- Product/PMs owning onboarding funnels
- SRE/Platform for operational guardrails

Decision matrix (one-page)

Use the table below to quickly classify customers and recommend a default migration pathway. Apply judgment when customers sit on a boundary — escalate to Solutions Eng Lead.

| Customer characteristic | Primary recommended path | Why / key considerations | Minimum SLO targets to require this path |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Low volume PoC (<= 1M tokens/month), developer-led | Remain Hosted (self-serve) | Fastest time-to-value; use dev credits and sandbox | 95th latency < 800ms, error rate < 0.5% |
| Predictable production traffic (1M–50M tokens/mo), data-sensitive | Dedicated (reserved capacity) | Predictable throughput and isolation; contractual SLAs | P95 latency < 350ms, availability 99.9% |
| Regulated workloads or on-prem compliance needs | Private (VPC / On‑prem) | Customer-managed networking/KMS; audit requirements | SLOs agreed per contract; baseline 99.95% availability |
| Burst-heavy, spiky sessions with tight tail latency needs | Dedicated with warm-burst and preemptible fallback | Combine reserved baseline + burst credits | P99 latency target < 800ms for bursts |
| Edge/low-region-variance needs (<50ms regional RT) | Edge light runtime (local cache) + Hybrid routing | Local prefetching + affinity routing | Regional P95 < 120ms |

Pre-migration checklist (operational, step-by-step)

1) Customer discovery & classification
   - Confirm peak tokens/day and tokens distribution by route. Export last 30 days from Console -> Usage -> Route summary.
   - Confirm data residency and retention policy. Capture contract clause requests.

2) Baseline telemetry and regression test bundle
   - Create a shadow-eval prompt set (10–20 prompts) that covers nominal and edge-case behaviors. Add to Shared Evals -> <customer-name>-pre-migration.json.
   - Run 48-hour synthetic traffic replay via consumption-sandbox runner (CLI):
     redwood sandbox run --customer-id <id> --replay-file replay-48h.json --target throughput 120%

3) Capacity planning & SKU proposal
   - Map observed P95 and CPU/GPU utilization to Dedicated SKU templates (see Appendix A). Recommend commit level and warm-burst allowance.

4) Security and compliance baseline
   - Confirm KMS/HSM provider and key rotation timing.
   - Verify audit log export path and retention length (default 90d).

5) Acceptance criteria and rollback window
   - Agree acceptance thresholds (latency, error, quality via shadow-evals) and initial canary duration (default: 72 hours).
   - Define rollback triggers: sustained 15% regression in accuracy on shadow-eval or 2x baseline error rate for 30 minutes.

Cost & latency simulation knobs (how to model choices)

- Batching profile: adjust mean batch size and target latency percentiles. Increasing batch size reduces per-token cost by ~12–25% for conversational workloads with median token length < 64, but increases P95 latency by ~50–200ms depending on the runtime kernel.
- Quantization level: fp16 -> int8 yields ~1.6–2.3x cost reduction; expect quality delta of 0.5–3% depending on model and prompt class (use shadow-evals).
- KV-cache retention: raising session KV lifetime can reduce repeated context costs; model cost reduction depends on prompt reuse.
- Warm-burst vs preemptible: reserved + warm-burst provides predictable P95; preemptible fallback reduces commit cost but requires careful SLO mapping and customer acceptance in contract.

Quick simulation example (CLI + JSON knobs)

1) Create a simulation input file sim-input.json (example):
{
  "monthly_tokens": 20000000,
  "avg_token_length": 45,
  "peak_rps": 120,
  "batch_profile": {"mean": 12, "max": 48},
  "quantization": "int8",
  "kv_retention_hours": 24
}

2) Run the offline estimator (developer sandbox):
   redwood cost-sim --input sim-input.json --region us-west-2 --sku-template dedicated-standard-8

This prints: estimated monthly spend, projected P95 latency, and quality delta vs hosted baseline. Include in proposal.

Phased rollout template (recommended default)

Phase 0: Planning (1–2 weeks) - Align on acceptance criteria, select SKU template, provision Dedicated cluster in customer region, prepare shadow-evals.
Phase 1: Canary (72–96 hours) - Route 2–5% of traffic to Dedicated cluster with continuous shadow-eval; monitor latency, error, and quality.
Phase 2: Ramp (1–2 weeks) - 20% -> 50% -> 100% staged routing; increase autoscaling buffer; re-run cost-sim with observed utilization.
Phase 3: Harden + Handover (1 week) - Finalize runbook, schedule SLO reviews (90d cadence), handover ops to customer success / support engineering.

Rollout monitoring dashboard (must-have metrics)
- P50/P95/P99 latency by route and model variant
- End-to-end error rate (5xx, 4xx) and retries
- Shadow-eval quality delta (loss or score change) with prompt breakdowns
- GPU utilization and queue times for batch windows
- Billing exposure estimate (real-time cost burn vs forecast)

Contract and negotiation quick points
- SLO mapping: propose P95 latency and availability targets tied to credits. Default: 99.9% availability for Dedicated Standard, 99.95% for Enterprise Dedicated with warm-burst.
- Burst credits: define monthly burst pool (tokens) and overage pricing.
- Fallback behavior: document which model variants will be used on preemptible fallback and notify customers of possible small quality deltas.
- Data processing clauses: include explicit language allowing telemetry export for performance debugging (anonymized by default).

Operational runbook snippet (incident triggers & immediate actions)
1) Trigger: P95 latency > 2x baseline for > 10 minutes - Action: Pause routing increments to Dedicated, scale up warm-burst if available, open incident, notify SE and SRE.
2) Trigger: Shadow-eval quality regression > 10% on critical prompt set - Action: Re-route traffic to Hosted fallback, revert to prior variant, open quality incident, engage Research/Applied ML.
3) Trigger: Cost burn > 150% of forecast for 60 minutes - Action: Throttle non-critical routes, alert finance/commercial owner, assess preemptible fallback to control spend.

Appendix A: SKU mapping cheatsheet (summary)
| Template | GPU | Typical sustained throughput (tokens/sec) | Suggested commit | Use case |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| dedicated-standard-4 | A10G | 800–1,200 | 2–4k USD / mo | Small to medium production routes |
| dedicated-standard-8 | A10G x2 | 1,600–2,400 | 6–12k USD / mo | Consistent medium workloads |
| dedicated-performance-16 | H100-class | 5,000–10,000 | 20k+ USD / mo | High throughput, low-latency transactional workloads |

Appendix B: Example acceptance criteria (copyable clause)
- Acceptance: During the 72-hour canary, Dedicated P95 latency shall not exceed Hosted baseline by more than 20%, and shadow-eval accuracy shall not degrade by more than 3% on the agreed prompt set. Failure to meet both conditions requires rollback and a joint remediation plan.
